newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Africa says coffee export cuts a survival matter.
newsitem.headline: Africa says coffee export cuts a survival matter.

text.p: The head of the InterAfrican Coffee Organisation (IACO) appealed passionately to Asian nations on Wednesday to join a plan to trim coffee exports, saying the issue was vital for African producers.

"Africa still has coffee as its lifeline," Guy-Alain Gauze, IACO chairman and Ivory Coast commodities minister, said in a speech at the Asia Coffee conference here. The speech was read for him by Ugandan Trade and Industry minister Abel Rwendeire.

Brazil and Colombia have agreed to back a plan to trim coffee exports by countries belonging to the 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) by more than 2.5 million 60-kg bags in the first half of 1997 to 23.7 million 60-kg bags from a previously projected 26.3 million bags.
The reduction plan will be presented in a special ACPC meeting in Rio de Janeiro next week.
"Now our appeal is to Asian countries to come on line," Gauze said. "In some (African) countries, 80-90 percent of foreign exchange earnings are from coffee...The African countries must survive."

The appeal is directed at Indonesia, an ACPC member and the biggest producer of coffee in Asia, and Vietnam, which is not a member of the group but has become a major producer of robusta coffee over the last few years.
Indonesia is the world's third biggest producer of coffee just behind Brazil and Colombia.
Gauze said coffee prices have declined sharply and partly blamed investment funds for causing the producers' problems.
"The situation is made worse by speculative funds that have come into play," he said. "We can not just take note of the crisis in the market and wait for better times to come."

IACO chief economist Donald Kaberuka told Reuters in an interview that African countries would present a selective reduction scheme at the ACPC meeting in Brazil, although the absence of major non-ACPC producers like Vietnam, Thailand and India is a "cause for concern."
"Basically, we're looking for their cooperation. As long as there is good compliance from Africa, Indonesia and Latin America, we believe this plan has good chances of success," Kaberuka said.
A selective reduction plan would be proposed which would affect both arabica and robusta volumes, "but the reduction will be relatively more important in robusta coffee".

Indonesia has expressed serious reservations about the plan because of the absence of Vietnam, but conference sources said the African nations would argue that the period covered by the scheme would not affect Indonesian exporters.

"By the end of January, Vietnam will have sold all of its robusta crop while Indonesia's crop will just be coming on stream in late March to April. This plan will not undercut them," a delegate at the conference said.
"This reduction is temporary. It will be reviewed once the price situation has improved," Kaberuka said
Delegates at the conference predicted a lot of hagggling in Brazil over the level of export cuts by each country.
Kaberuka also hinted at that. "The exact way of affecting the reduction and the volumes involved on the type of coffee will be subject to dicussion at the emergency meeting of the ACPC," he said.
Gauze, Rwendeire and Kaberuka will fly to Hanoi later this week to hand in a letter to the government calling on Vietnam to join the ACPC.
